name: Esther Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Esther. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is kept confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Linden Medical Supply. We're a wholesaler, so we buy bandages, gloves, syringes, thermometers and everyday medicines like paracetamol, and sell them to pharmacies and care homes. My mornings are checking stock against what the care homes usually need, and my afternoons are calls with manufacturers about prices and delivery dates. Everything has batch numbers and expiry dates, so there's a lot of careful checking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy that it matters. If a care home runs out of gloves, real people suffer, and I like being the buyer who prevents that. What wears me down is the recalls, when a batch is pulled and I have to trace every box. I use the AI assistant our company bought now and then, mostly to summarise long supplier contracts, once a colleague showed me it was reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds quite restful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the summaries got faster and that's about it. With friends after church I'd say you still need careful people when it's medicine. I'm not really online, maybe a photo of a cake now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is safe and my plans hold. Samuel, my husband, is a paramedic, we own a small house with a modest mortgage, and I've got good savings. We'd like to start a family in the next couple of years, and this picture lets us do that without worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the same way and use the assistant for contracts. I'd keep putting money into savings each month for when the baby comes. Maybe I'd do the compliance course my manager mentioned, because it leads to a better grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even with AI stalling, is anything on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samuel's shifts, mostly. Twelve hours, nights, it wears him out. Whether we can manage on one and a half incomes when we have children is a real worry, but an ordinary one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the compliance course. What is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a qualification in medicines regulation, the rules about storing and selling medicine safely. Linden pays for half. It would put me in line for the senior buyer job in a few years.

say: I'd say the **summaries** got faster and that's about it.
I'd tell friends you still need **careful people** when it's medicine.
think: My **job is safe** and our plans hold.
With a paramedic husband, a **small house** and savings, we can start a family.
do: Keep using the assistant for **contracts** only.
Take the **compliance course**, half paid by Linden.
S0.quote: Whether we can manage on one and a half incomes when we have children is a real worry, but an ordinary one.
fieldNote: Esther ties her work to **care homes and patients**, which gives it meaning.
Her ordinary worries are **Samuel's night shifts** and managing on less with children.
She sees **regulation** as a reason careful people stay needed.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant to summarise supplier contracts
Save a set amount monthly toward the first baby
Sign up for the medicines regulation course Linden half pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and checking. That's quite a lot of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should use it carefully, because a mistake with medicine isn't like a mistake with cardboard. With friends I'd say jobs like mine will change, but someone still has to sign off. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the routine reordering goes to AI and the team of five shrinks to three or four over a few years. The recall work and the compliance checks keep a person in the loop, because the law says someone has to be responsible. I think I'd be one of those kept, but I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which tools the bigger wholesalers use and then learn those properly, maybe within a year. I'd do the compliance course straight away, because that's the part a person still signs. And I'd keep saving, no big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'm alright, but I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably be kept. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the one who handles recalls. When the gloves batch was pulled last spring, I traced four hundred boxes across sixty care homes, and managers remember who did that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not in this picture. Maybe I'd wait until after the compliance course, so I'm in a stronger spot. But Samuel's job is hands-on, so we'd still feel steady.

say: I'd say a **medicine mistake** isn't like a mistake with cardboard.
I'd tell friends someone still has to **sign off**.
think: Routine reordering goes to AI and the team shrinks to **three or four**.
Recalls and **compliance checks** keep a person responsible by law.
do: Learn the tools the **big wholesalers** adopt, within a year.
S1.quote: When the gloves batch was pulled last spring, I traced four hundred boxes across sixty care homes, and managers remember who did that.
fieldNote: Esther believes **legal responsibility** protects her part of the job.
She waits for **proven tools** before learning them, fitting her steady style.
Her husband's **hands-on job** makes the household feel steady.

steps.text: Learn the buying tools once the big wholesalers prove them
Start the medicines regulation course this term
Watch which roles Linden cuts before making bigger moves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast. I'd be twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we must keep a person responsible for medicines, whatever the machines can do. With friends I'd say we need to look after each other, families and churches especially. I might share something about it, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think buying goes, even the compliance part, if the AI can do any thinking work. The law would probably catch up within a year or two. Samuel would be fine longer, ambulances need hands until 2031 at least, but I'd lose my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a pharmacy technician course straight away, because that's measuring, checking and handing medicine to people, which is hands-on. We'd cut back, no new car, smaller holiday. And we'd think hard about whether to have a baby now, while I'm still employed and on maternity pay, or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, we'd have Samuel's wage and savings. But I'd lose something I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd think about having a baby now. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if my buying job is going anyway, having a baby now and coming back to retrain might make sense. My mother did that, she stayed home five years. It's not the worst plan if we've got Samuel's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our church, my parents, Samuel's family. We'd manage without the government if we could. That's how my parents did it when they first arrived.

say: I'd insist a person stays **responsible for medicines**.
I'd tell friends **families and churches** should look after each other.
think: Buying goes, **even compliance**, once AI can do any thinking work.
Samuel's job lasts longer, but **my income** would go.
do: Start a **pharmacy technician** course straight away.
Cut back with **no new car** and a smaller holiday.
Decide whether to **have a baby now** while still employed.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, because Samuel's wage and **savings** remain.
S2.quote: If my buying job is going anyway, having a baby now and coming back to retrain might make sense.
fieldNote: Esther expects to **lose her income** but leans on her husband's hands-on job.
She reframes job loss as a chance to **bring family plans forward**.
She prefers **church and family** support to government help.

steps.text: Enrol in a pharmacy technician course this year
Skip the new car and book a smaller holiday
Talk with Samuel about having a baby this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, 2031. And robots in 2034. That's a little gentler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we have time to train people for the hands-on jobs in medicine. With friends I'd say it's coming, so plan your family and your work together. Nothing much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still expect buying to end in 2031. But five years means I can have a baby, go back, and then move into something hands-on like pharmacy technician work before it lands. I'd be thirty-two, which feels fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish the compliance course and learn the AI tools Linden brings in, so I'm useful until the end. I'd start planning for a baby in the next year or two. And I'd look at the pharmacy technician course for after maternity leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Calmer than the fast one, but still my job ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn AI tools in a job you think is ending. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want a good reference and the maternity pay. Leaving well matters, and my father always said, finish the work in front of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are pharmacy technicians safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever, I suppose. But there's a lot of talking to people, checking, being responsible. I'd guess that lasts past 2034 in some form.

say: I'd say there's time to train people for **hands-on medicine** jobs.
I'd tell friends to plan **family and work** together.
think: Five years allows a **baby**, a return, and a move into pharmacy work.
do: Finish the compliance course and learn **Linden's AI tools**.
Plan for **a baby** in the next year or two.
Line up the **pharmacy technician** course after maternity leave.
feel: **Anxious**, calmer than two years but **still** my job ending.
S3.quote: Leaving well matters, and my father always said, finish the work in front of you.
fieldNote: Esther plans to **learn the tools** while expecting the job to end.
Her plan weaves **family and career** together in a set order.
Her father's saying shapes her **sense of duty** at work.

steps.text: Learn Linden's new AI buying tools well enough to train others
Plan a first baby with Samuel within two years
Book a pharmacy technician course for after maternity leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this gives everyone time, and companies should use it to retrain staff properly. With friends I'd say it's the same news, just with time to be sensible. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels manageable. We'd have children, I'd have time at home, and I could come back into something hands-on. I'd be thirty-seven when buying ends, and I'd want to be settled in new work by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal for now and take the senior buyer job if it comes. We'd have our first child in the next couple of years, as planned. Around year four or five I'd start the pharmacy technician training, once I see what's holding up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it doesn't stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start sooner than year four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Linden stopped replacing buyers who leave. Or if the law changed so AI could sign off on medicines. Those would be my signals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Samuel's job change how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. He'll be needed in an ambulance until 2039 at least, probably longer. Knowing my husband has a hands-on ambulance job takes most of the fear out.

say: I'd say companies should use the time to **retrain staff** properly.
I'd call it the **same news** with time to be sensible.
think: Ten years feels **manageable** with children and a return to work.
I'd want to be in **new work** by thirty-seven.

S4.quote: Knowing my husband has a hands-on ambulance job takes most of the fear out.
fieldNote: Esther's calm rests heavily on **Samuel's ambulance job**.

steps.text: Apply for the senior buyer job at Linden if offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough time to plan a family and a new career. What would help is employers paying for retraining while people still work, and keeping maternity rights strong, so women like me don't have to choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about responsibility. With medicine, someone has to answer when it goes wrong, and I'd want to know who that is when the AI is buying.

headlineQuote: With medicine, someone has to answer when it goes wrong, and I'd want to know who that is when the AI is buying.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old medical supplies** buyer, married to Samuel, a paramedic.
She uses AI **now and then**, after colleagues prove it, mostly for contract summaries.
She believes **legal responsibility** for medicines keeps people in the loop for a while.
Her husband's **hands-on job** steadies her, so she's anxious rather than alarmed when AGI comes fast.
She plans to **have children** and then move into pharmacy technician work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, too fast to plan a family and a new career.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while working, and strong **maternity rights**.
